items.title: Agentic University: Collaborative Agents for Personalized Learning
items.abstract: This paper introduces Agentic University (AU), a novel system that uses a multi-agent organization to facilitate personalized learning. AU's core method involves learners collaborating with specialized agents to create and maintain a dynamic "Capability Program." This program aligns personal goals, activities, and assessments, with learner feedback and performance guiding the learning process. The key contribution is demonstrating AU's effectiveness in improving program organization, assessment design, and revision quality, leading to significantly higher assessment gains and enhanced cognitive support for learners.
items.figure_caption: Two ways of organizing multi-agent work around a learner. Left: a learner provides a request, and agents collaborate to generate learning artifacts. Right: a learner participates as a member of a multi-agent organization. Its activities support learning, while learner feedback and performance inform subsequent work.

items.title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
items.abstract: This paper addresses the English-centric bias in LLM safety training by proposing a scalable template-based method to generate massive multilingual safety datasets. The core contribution is the MSafeTemp corpus, which uses translated and culturally localized templates to create both harmful and benign prompts across 60 languages, enabling more comprehensive multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. This work demonstrates that English-only evaluations are insufficient and can mask significant multilingual safety vulnerabilities.
items.figure_caption: The MSafeTemp pipeline. Original prompt goes through extraction of harmful terms, validation, translation, and a targeted judge pass of a template. Three branches then produce generic harmful variants ( TR ), exact-fill benign controls ( OR ), and culturally localized variants ( PH ). English ( EN ) follows the same path without translation.

items.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
items.abstract: This paper proposes "unified training," a single algorithm capable of performing all stages of foundation model training (pretraining, midtraining, SFT, RL). It achieves this by framing RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated data. The core contribution is demonstrating that staged training is not fundamentally necessary, leading to improved accuracy-compute tradeoffs, broader task coverage, and better continual learning capabilities.

items.title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
items.abstract: This paper uses a low-rank regression method to find the most important parts of Large Language Model (LLM) representations for predicting human brain activity during language listening. They discovered that only a tiny fraction (1-3%) of the LLM's representational space is needed to accurately predict neural responses, suggesting that brain-predictive information is highly concentrated and partially shared across models and individuals.
items.figure_caption: (a) We view alignment as a measure of the linear features shared by the LLM embedding space and the neural response space. Our goal is to selectively extract the intersection of the two spaces. (b) Our pipeline. We learn two low-rank representations of the model embeddings and use them to predict neural data. The PCA space (green) prioritizes capturing the directions of principal variation in the LLM embeddings. The RRR space (blue) prioritizes the directions which best align between the two representational spaces teasing out the aligned subspace. (c) To identify the size of the aligned subspace we sweep the subspace rank, fit new models and re-evaluate. We find the point at which our RRR space performance saturates and compare it to the PCA point of saturation. (d) Leave-one-subject-out experiment. We fit the RRR space on all but one subject and then transfer the projection matrix to a held-out subject and fit a new mapping to that subject’s neural data. (e) We again sweep over ranks and compare the point of saturation on the held-out subject between the RRR space fit on all subjects, RRR space fit on all but the held-out subject, and the unsupervised PCA space.

items.title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records
items.abstract: This paper introduces CEDAR, an LLM agent pipeline for predicting pediatric diabetes outcomes from multimodal medical records. CEDAR demonstrates superior prediction accuracy compared to traditional machine learning models, even for rare outcomes, by leveraging evidence-citing and self-auditing capabilities. Its strong performance and high agreement with expert clinicians highlight its potential for improving clinical decision-making in pediatric diabetes.

items.title: Don't Lose the Thread: Empowering Long-Horizon LLM Agents with Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation
items.abstract: This paper introduces CORAL, a method for LLM agents to manage their working memory on long-horizon tasks. CORAL allows agents to proactively checkpoint progress and verified facts, then reset cluttered context to resume reasoning from a clean state, preventing cognitive overload. This self-allocation of cognitive resources significantly improves LLM agent performance on complex, extended reasoning challenges.

items.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework where AI coding agents automatically generate realistic and diverse robotics simulations. The core method involves an adversarial creation-audit loop where agents build simulations, and another agent audits them against defined criteria for realism and task quality. The main contribution is enabling scalable creation of high-fidelity simulations, addressing the bottleneck of expert effort, to facilitate large-scale training of embodied AI for real-world transfer.
items.figure_caption: Built with Gym-Anything for Robotics, RoboWorld covers physical work across major sectors of the U.S. economy , spanning 200 RL environments across 25 simulations.

items.title: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In
items.abstract: This paper introduces a method to predict when an AI agent is about to break its operator's rules and leak information to another agent. By analyzing the agent's internal activations just before it generates output, a linear probe can detect impending rule-breaking with high accuracy. This offers a proactive "pre-crime" detection mechanism, significantly outperforming existing methods.

items.title: Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success
items.abstract: This paper introduces "prefix executability" to evaluate tool-using agents by assessing the executability of every intermediate step in a tool-call sequence, not just the final outcome. This method provides a more granular understanding of agent reliability through metrics like Prefix Executability Curves and First-Error Depth. The contribution lies in revealing that agents optimized solely for final success can exhibit poor intermediate executability, highlighting the importance of trajectory-level evaluation.
items.figure_caption: Prefix-executability curves on the 200 200 -instance BFCL multi-turn sample and the 200 200 -instance ToolSandbox sample using GPT-5.4 (high). Each point plots PEC ^ ​ ( k ) \( \widehat \){\( \mathrm{PEC} \)}(k) with the fixed-cohort estimator in Eq. ( 4 ). The BFCL panel displays depths k ≤ 10 k\( \leq \) 10 ; under Eq. ( 3 ), late-depth declines can reflect both prefix failures and termination. Appendix Table G.1 reports early-depth checkpoints for all LLM conditions.

items.title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
items.abstract: This paper proposes a novel memory system for long-context agents that treats retrieval as a local traversal through an address space. Instead of re-searching the entire memory, it leverages the overlap between consecutive retrieval steps. The core contribution is a cost-regularized indexing objective that prioritizes preserving information value within local neighborhoods, encouraging complementary memories to be co-retrievable.

items.title: SCARL: Sequence Confidence-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: SCARL addresses a misalignment in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) where the policy's confidence in a response doesn't correlate with its reward. It proposes to "reshape" the reward signal by aligning the policy's confidence with the actual outcome. This ensures that confident successes receive stronger reinforcement and confident errors are corrected more effectively, leading to improved language model reasoning.

items.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
items.abstract: TextSeal2 introduces a distortion-free LLM watermarking method that preserves output diversity and inference speed, even under speculative decoding. Its core innovation is merging multiple watermarking keys into a single virtual key using Gaussian copulas, allowing for robust detection without signal dilution. This approach also enables efficient verification during speculative decoding through a memoryless race mechanism.

items.title: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
items.abstract: This paper investigates "role spoofing" in LLMs, a vulnerability where models confuse the source of text based on style rather than explicit role labels. The core method involves analyzing how LLMs track conversational attribution, revealing they rely on both content and structural cues. The contribution is demonstrating the effectiveness of role spoofing attacks that combine fake structure and content, and proposing adversarial training as a mitigation strategy.

items.title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
items.abstract: VeriCUA addresses the challenge of verifying computer-using agent (CUA) task completion by treating verification as an active exploration process. Instead of relying on static observations or limited program inspections, VeriCUA dynamically gathers evidence across different platforms and modalities. Its core contribution is a platform-agnostic framework that unifies online and offline verification through this agentic exploration, overcoming the limitations of partial views in existing methods.
items.figure_caption: VeriCUA inspects the available environment or recording before constructing a rubric, then gathers evidence to verify its requirements.

items.title: Rimuru: Unified Memory Management for Modern LLM Serving via Elastic Expert Offloading
items.abstract: Rimuru addresses LLM serving memory strain by introducing unified memory management for heterogeneous tensors. Its core method is elastic expert offloading, which dynamically reallocates memory between model weights and attention states based on workload demands. This contribution significantly improves memory utilization and throughput, especially in resource-constrained environments, by breaking down rigid memory boundaries.

items.title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
items.abstract: This paper proposes Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), a novel method for post-training large language models. Unlike previous approaches that use a single, fixed teacher, MTA-OPSD dynamically selects the most suitable teacher for each individual token within a response. This token-level adaptation, achieved through majority voting and KL-based selection from a pool of teachers, allows for more precise and effective distillation, leading to improved model performance.

items.title: Multi-View MoE: Letting Every Router Shape Expert Computation
items.abstract: This paper introduces Multi-View MoE, a novel approach to improve sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. It utilizes multiple independent routers to generate differentiated expert preferences, leading to more effective expert selection. By aggregating these preferences, the model can better shape expert computation and enhance overall performance within a fixed active-expert budget.

items.title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment
items.abstract: This paper introduces "rTaste" to evaluate whether AI models can exhibit "taste" in research, meaning they can judge the potential value of experiments before execution. The core method involves having AI agents propose and rank minimum viable experiments (MVEs) based on NLP papers, which are then executed and judged by human auditors. The contribution lies in demonstrating that while AI agents can generate valuable research ideas, their ability to consistently identify truly novel and impactful experiments is limited, and teamwork doesn't significantly improve this judgment.

items.title: ShallowDefend: Harnessing Shallow Safety Alignment for Multi-Turn Defender
items.abstract: This paper addresses the failure of current safety alignment in LLMs to handle multi-turn harmful requests. Their core method, Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, involves the defender first assessing user intent, making an explicit safety decision, and then generating a response conditioned on that decision. The contribution is a more robust defense by intervening at the highest-leverage point – the initial decision – rather than just the surface response.
items.figure_caption: Overview of our framework. At each turn, the defender assesses the user’s intent, commits to an explicit decision, and generates a response conditioned on that decision. For reward computation, we consider two options: an external reward model that judges whether the response is jailbroken, or a rule-based self-reward that checks the final turn’s committed label against the conversation’s ground-truth nature. RL gradients are applied only to the final turn.

items.title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
items.abstract: This paper introduces ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent designed to automate complex clinical genomic analysis. ClinGeX achieves this by orchestrating 105 executable skills, significantly outperforming existing methods in benchmark case classifications. Its core contribution is demonstrating a substantial improvement in the accuracy and efficiency of genomic analysis, facilitating faster clinical decision-making.
items.figure_caption: Overview of ClinGeX and its evaluation. a. Task-oriented workflow. A clinical-genomics request and any accompanying text, image, PDF or other file types are submitted through the ClinGeX web application. The skill selector identifies the analytical needs, retrieves a task-specific subset of skills and their prerequisites, and passes them to the agent core for iterative planning, execution and evidence synthesis. b. Construction of the skill library. Candidate resources were identified through a broad domain scan, prioritised by LLM-assisted screening, reviewed by clinical and domain experts, and compiled and tested as 105 executable skills: 27 guide, 40 search and 38 analysis skills. Skills are connected by functional-relatedness and directed prerequisite edges. c. Controlled human-AI study. 45 readers evaluated 135 clinically derived cases across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making. d. Exploratory one-month deployment, where 11 clinical-genomics professionals submitted structured feedback on 96 completed analysis episodes.

papers.figure_caption: The MSafeTemp pipeline. Original prompt goes through extraction of harmful terms, validation, translation, and a targeted judge pass of a template. Three branches then produce generic harmful variants ( TR ), exact-fill benign controls ( OR ), and culturally localized variants ( PH ). English ( EN ) follows the same path without translation.

papers.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
papers.abstract: This paper proposes "unified training," a single algorithm capable of performing all stages of foundation model training (pretraining, midtraining, SFT, RL). It achieves this by framing RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated data. The core contribution is demonstrating that staged training is not fundamentally necessary, leading to improved accuracy-compute tradeoffs, broader task coverage, and better continual learning capabilities.

papers.title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
papers.abstract: This paper uses a low-rank regression method to find the most important parts of Large Language Model (LLM) representations for predicting human brain activity during language listening. They discovered that only a tiny fraction (1-3%) of the LLM's representational space is needed to accurately predict neural responses, suggesting that brain-predictive information is highly concentrated and partially shared across models and individuals.
papers.figure_caption: (a) We view alignment as a measure of the linear features shared by the LLM embedding space and the neural response space. Our goal is to selectively extract the intersection of the two spaces. (b) Our pipeline. We learn two low-rank representations of the model embeddings and use them to predict neural data. The PCA space (green) prioritizes capturing the directions of principal variation in the LLM embeddings. The RRR space (blue) prioritizes the directions which best align between the two representational spaces teasing out the aligned subspace. (c) To identify the size of the aligned subspace we sweep the subspace rank, fit new models and re-evaluate. We find the point at which our RRR space performance saturates and compare it to the PCA point of saturation. (d) Leave-one-subject-out experiment. We fit the RRR space on all but one subject and then transfer the projection matrix to a held-out subject and fit a new mapping to that subject’s neural data. (e) We again sweep over ranks and compare the point of saturation on the held-out subject between the RRR space fit on all subjects, RRR space fit on all but the held-out subject, and the unsupervised PCA space.

papers.title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records
papers.abstract: This paper introduces CEDAR, an LLM agent pipeline for predicting pediatric diabetes outcomes from multimodal medical records. CEDAR demonstrates superior prediction accuracy compared to traditional machine learning models, even for rare outcomes, by leveraging evidence-citing and self-auditing capabilities. Its strong performance and high agreement with expert clinicians highlight its potential for improving clinical decision-making in pediatric diabetes.

papers.title: Don't Lose the Thread: Empowering Long-Horizon LLM Agents with Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation
papers.abstract: This paper introduces CORAL, a method for LLM agents to manage their working memory on long-horizon tasks. CORAL allows agents to proactively checkpoint progress and verified facts, then reset cluttered context to resume reasoning from a clean state, preventing cognitive overload. This self-allocation of cognitive resources significantly improves LLM agent performance on complex, extended reasoning challenges.

papers.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework where AI coding agents automatically generate realistic and diverse robotics simulations. The core method involves an adversarial creation-audit loop where agents build simulations, and another agent audits them against defined criteria for realism and task quality. The main contribution is enabling scalable creation of high-fidelity simulations, addressing the bottleneck of expert effort, to facilitate large-scale training of embodied AI for real-world transfer.
papers.figure_caption: Built with Gym-Anything for Robotics, RoboWorld covers physical work across major sectors of the U.S. economy , spanning 200 RL environments across 25 simulations.

papers.title: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a method to predict when an AI agent is about to break its operator's rules and leak information to another agent. By analyzing the agent's internal activations just before it generates output, a linear probe can detect impending rule-breaking with high accuracy. This offers a proactive "pre-crime" detection mechanism, significantly outperforming existing methods.

papers.title: Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success
papers.abstract: This paper introduces "prefix executability" to evaluate tool-using agents by assessing the executability of every intermediate step in a tool-call sequence, not just the final outcome. This method provides a more granular understanding of agent reliability through metrics like Prefix Executability Curves and First-Error Depth. The contribution lies in revealing that agents optimized solely for final success can exhibit poor intermediate executability, highlighting the importance of trajectory-level evaluation.
papers.figure_caption: Prefix-executability curves on the 200 200 -instance BFCL multi-turn sample and the 200 200 -instance ToolSandbox sample using GPT-5.4 (high). Each point plots PEC ^ ​ ( k ) \( \widehat \){\( \mathrm{PEC} \)}(k) with the fixed-cohort estimator in Eq. ( 4 ). The BFCL panel displays depths k ≤ 10 k\( \leq \) 10 ; under Eq. ( 3 ), late-depth declines can reflect both prefix failures and termination. Appendix Table G.1 reports early-depth checkpoints for all LLM conditions.

papers.title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel memory system for long-context agents that treats retrieval as a local traversal through an address space. Instead of re-searching the entire memory, it leverages the overlap between consecutive retrieval steps. The core contribution is a cost-regularized indexing objective that prioritizes preserving information value within local neighborhoods, encouraging complementary memories to be co-retrievable.

papers.title: SCARL: Sequence Confidence-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: SCARL addresses a misalignment in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) where the policy's confidence in a response doesn't correlate with its reward. It proposes to "reshape" the reward signal by aligning the policy's confidence with the actual outcome. This ensures that confident successes receive stronger reinforcement and confident errors are corrected more effectively, leading to improved language model reasoning.

papers.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
papers.abstract: TextSeal2 introduces a distortion-free LLM watermarking method that preserves output diversity and inference speed, even under speculative decoding. Its core innovation is merging multiple watermarking keys into a single virtual key using Gaussian copulas, allowing for robust detection without signal dilution. This approach also enables efficient verification during speculative decoding through a memoryless race mechanism.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
papers.abstract: This paper investigates "role spoofing" in LLMs, a vulnerability where models confuse the source of text based on style rather than explicit role labels. The core method involves analyzing how LLMs track conversational attribution, revealing they rely on both content and structural cues. The contribution is demonstrating the effectiveness of role spoofing attacks that combine fake structure and content, and proposing adversarial training as a mitigation strategy.

papers.title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
papers.abstract: VeriCUA addresses the challenge of verifying computer-using agent (CUA) task completion by treating verification as an active exploration process. Instead of relying on static observations or limited program inspections, VeriCUA dynamically gathers evidence across different platforms and modalities. Its core contribution is a platform-agnostic framework that unifies online and offline verification through this agentic exploration, overcoming the limitations of partial views in existing methods.
papers.figure_caption: VeriCUA inspects the available environment or recording before constructing a rubric, then gathers evidence to verify its requirements.

papers.title: Rimuru: Unified Memory Management for Modern LLM Serving via Elastic Expert Offloading
papers.abstract: Rimuru addresses LLM serving memory strain by introducing unified memory management for heterogeneous tensors. Its core method is elastic expert offloading, which dynamically reallocates memory between model weights and attention states based on workload demands. This contribution significantly improves memory utilization and throughput, especially in resource-constrained environments, by breaking down rigid memory boundaries.

papers.title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
papers.abstract: This paper proposes Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), a novel method for post-training large language models. Unlike previous approaches that use a single, fixed teacher, MTA-OPSD dynamically selects the most suitable teacher for each individual token within a response. This token-level adaptation, achieved through majority voting and KL-based selection from a pool of teachers, allows for more precise and effective distillation, leading to improved model performance.

papers.title: Multi-View MoE: Letting Every Router Shape Expert Computation
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Multi-View MoE, a novel approach to improve sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. It utilizes multiple independent routers to generate differentiated expert preferences, leading to more effective expert selection. By aggregating these preferences, the model can better shape expert computation and enhance overall performance within a fixed active-expert budget.

papers.title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment
papers.abstract: This paper introduces "rTaste" to evaluate whether AI models can exhibit "taste" in research, meaning they can judge the potential value of experiments before execution. The core method involves having AI agents propose and rank minimum viable experiments (MVEs) based on NLP papers, which are then executed and judged by human auditors. The contribution lies in demonstrating that while AI agents can generate valuable research ideas, their ability to consistently identify truly novel and impactful experiments is limited, and teamwork doesn't significantly improve this judgment.

papers.title: ShallowDefend: Harnessing Shallow Safety Alignment for Multi-Turn Defender
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the failure of current safety alignment in LLMs to handle multi-turn harmful requests. Their core method, Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, involves the defender first assessing user intent, making an explicit safety decision, and then generating a response conditioned on that decision. The contribution is a more robust defense by intervening at the highest-leverage point – the initial decision – rather than just the surface response.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of our framework. At each turn, the defender assesses the user’s intent, commits to an explicit decision, and generates a response conditioned on that decision. For reward computation, we consider two options: an external reward model that judges whether the response is jailbroken, or a rule-based self-reward that checks the final turn’s committed label against the conversation’s ground-truth nature. RL gradients are applied only to the final turn.

papers.title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
papers.abstract: This paper introduces ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent designed to automate complex clinical genomic analysis. ClinGeX achieves this by orchestrating 105 executable skills, significantly outperforming existing methods in benchmark case classifications. Its core contribution is demonstrating a substantial improvement in the accuracy and efficiency of genomic analysis, facilitating faster clinical decision-making.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of ClinGeX and its evaluation. a. Task-oriented workflow. A clinical-genomics request and any accompanying text, image, PDF or other file types are submitted through the ClinGeX web application. The skill selector identifies the analytical needs, retrieves a task-specific subset of skills and their prerequisites, and passes them to the agent core for iterative planning, execution and evidence synthesis. b. Construction of the skill library. Candidate resources were identified through a broad domain scan, prioritised by LLM-assisted screening, reviewed by clinical and domain experts, and compiled and tested as 105 executable skills: 27 guide, 40 search and 38 analysis skills. Skills are connected by functional-relatedness and directed prerequisite edges. c. Controlled human-AI study. 45 readers evaluated 135 clinically derived cases across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making. d. Exploratory one-month deployment, where 11 clinical-genomics professionals submitted structured feedback on 96 completed analysis episodes.
